newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge hardliners a threat despite woes.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge hardliners a threat despite woes.

text.p: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge rebels have been battered by a major split in their ranks, a series of defections and territorial losses but hardliners loyal to Pol Pot will remain a threat for some time, military analysts said.
"They remain a considerable force to be reckoned with," a Western military analyst said, adding that the hardliners had enough arms and ammunition "to create problems for many years to come".
He estimated their strength at 3,000-4,000 based around the northern stronghold of Anlong Veng and a further 1,000-2,000 around Veal Veng and other southwestern pockets.

A military attache agreed that the rebels would remain a potent threat despite the severe setback of the August breakaway of significant forces in the northwest and the defection of hundreds of guerrillas to the government since October 1.
"There are still quite a number. They still have everything necessary to pursue their fight," he said of loyalists to hardline leader Pol Pot.
"It can still be a long fight," he told Reuters, adding: "They are not going to win any big battles against the royal government, but they can still resist and occupy their zone."

The Khmer Rouge, blamed for the deaths of more than one million people during the 1975-79 "killing fields" rule, signed a peace pact in 1991 but reneged on the accord and have been fighting the government formed in 1993.

Some analysts believe the splintering of the Maoist-inspired guerrilla movement could, ironically, pose a new threat by further polarising the fragile royal coalition government, with rival parties seeking the loyalty of different Khmer Rouge factions.

The split between Khmer Rouge hardliners and dissident leader Ieng Sary, foreign minister during Khmer Rouge rule, had helped to paper over a rift between co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen over power-sharing.
But the analysts believed tensions had resurfaced along with growing signs of impatience, especially from Hun Sen, at the slow process of reconciliation with Ieng Sary's force of up to 4,000.
"They just seem to be contributing to the polarisation (of the political scene)," the military analyst said of the defectors and Ieng Sary's forces.

"They virtually have to make up their minds one way or the other who they're going to be associated with," he said, adding that the Ieng Sary group seemed to be closer to royalist Ranariddh while defectors from southwestern areas were siding with Hun Sen.
Government officials do not acknowledge such problems and remain publicly upbeat about the reconciliation process.

Co-Defence Minister Tea Banh, who on Sunday presided over an army induction ceremony for representatives of eight hardline Khmer Rouge divisions in the southwest, said the days of the Maoist-faction were numbered.
"We can't say this year or next year will be the end of the Khmer Rouge, but I think their activities are stepping down day (by) day and will disappear very soon," he told Reuters.

Defence Ministry Secretary of State Ek Sereyvath estimated hardline forces at "just below 1,000 fighters" and he believed Pol Pot had summoned all loyalist guerrillas to Anlong Veng after the setbacks elsewhere.
Ieng Sary's fighters compounded the problems of the hardliners on September 30 by taking over the Samlaut area, scene of a 1967 peasant uprising and their last toehold in the northwest.
He has yet to merge his forces with the government but has forged a ceasefire pact and analysts believe the recent defections could put pressure on Ieng Sary to complete the reconciliation.
Another military analyst believed the defections and the split by Ieng Sary marked "the end of the Khmer Rouge in the northwest and the southwest".
"In the north, maybe, they can survive one more dry season," he told Reuters, asserting: "They are finished as a guerrilla force whose aim is to destabilise the country and gain power.
"These defectors are like rats fleeing the sinking ship...one day it will sink totally, that's for sure," he added.
